idiom_name: typed props interfaces on function components
implementation_notes: TypeScript makes the relay visible: every intermediate must declare the forwarded prop in its own props type, so the compiler forces the chain to be written down and a reshape of the value breaks the build at each level instead of silently mis-forwarding. That is its strength (traceability, safe renames) and the reason deep chains hurt - each intermediate's type grows a field it never reads. Keep each props type minimal and pass elements/children where a layer only places the consumer.
pitfalls: Marking a relayed value optional (`user?: User`) pushes the missing-prop failure into a leaf at runtime; keep required data required in the consumer's props type.
Typing an intermediate's props as a broad shared state or `any` defeats the compiler's ability to show that the component forwards what it does not use.

variants.name: Typed context with a throwing accessor hook
variants.idiom_name: createContext<T | null>(null) plus a useX() hook that throws
variants.implementation_notes: The typed form of the context remedy: declare the context with an explicit type (`createContext<Auth | null>(null)`) and wrap `useContext` in a small hook that throws when no provider is present, so the compiler tracks the value's type at every consumer and a missing provider fails loudly instead of returning null deep in the tree. `@types/react` supplies the generics for provider props and hooks; memoise the provider value exactly as in plain JavaScript.
pitfalls: A context typed as `T | null` without a throwing accessor pushes a null check into every consumer - the type no longer expresses the invariant.
Untyped `createContext({})` defaults produce a context whose value shape drifts silently; always parameterise the generic.
